**The Second Draft**

Consider the octopus, an animal that solves mazes, opens jars, and escapes through holes the size of its eyeball—yet does much of its thinking outside its brain. Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons live in its arms. Each arm can taste, touch, and, to some degree, decide, semi-independent of the central brain. It is as if you could detach your hand and watch it continue to explore the world on its own.

Their skin is stranger still. An octopus can change color and texture in a fraction of a second, matching coral, sand, or kelp. And the skin itself may be light-sensitive: it contains opsins, the same family of proteins that build sight in eyes. Some scientists suspect an octopus doesn't just wear its camouflage—it may, in some dim sense, see through it.

Then there is sleep. Researchers once filmed a sleeping octopus whose skin flushed through waves of color, cycling through hues resembling the REM sleep of dreaming mammals. No one knows what, if anything, an octopus dreams. But the image is hard to shake: a creature alone in a dark tank, its skin flickering through landscapes it may be visiting only in its mind.

We tend to measure intelligence by resemblance to ourselves—tool use, faces, speech. The octopus fails almost every one of those tests and passes others we barely know how to give. And mind is not a single invention. Evolution tried it more than once, and the second draft looks nothing like the first.

Severed from the body, an arm will still reach and grasp. It is as if you could detach your hand and watch it continue to explore the world on its own.

Their skin is stranger still. An octopus can change color and texture in a fraction of a second, matching coral, sand, or kelp with astonishing precision. And the skin itself may be light-sensitive: it contains opsins, the same family of proteins that build sight in eyes. Some scientists suspect an octopus doesn't just wear its camouflage—it may, in some dim sense, see through it.

Then there is sleep. In 2021, researchers filmed a sleeping octopus whose skin flushed through waves of color and pattern, cycling through hues in a way that resembled the REM sleep of dreaming mammals. No one knows what, if anything, an octopus dreams. But the image is hard to shake: a creature alone in a dark tank, its skin flickering through landscapes it may be visiting only in its mind.

We tend to measure intelligence by resemblance to ourselves—tool use, faces, speech. The octopus fails almost every one of those tests and passes others we barely know how to give. It is a reminder that mind is not a single invention. Evolution tried it more than once, and the second draft looks nothing like the first."
